For an integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathbf1_n\in\mathbb R^n$ be the vector whose entries are all $1$, and let $I_n$ be the $n\times n$ identity matrix. The **centering matrix** is

$$H_n:=I_n-\frac1n\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T.$$

For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\bar v:=n^{-1}\mathbf1_n^Tv$; then $H_nv=v-\bar v\mathbf1_n$. For a finite data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $p\ge1$, its **centered data matrix** is $X_c:=H_nX$; each column of $X_c$ has sum zero.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

derivations.claim: The matrix $\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$ is symmetric, so the formula in [F1] gives $H_n^T=H_n$. Also $\mathbf1_n^T\mathbf1_n=n$, and hence $H_n\mathbf1_n=\mathbf1_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n n=0$.

Writing $J=\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$, one has $J^2=\mathbf1_n(\mathbf1_n^T\mathbf1_n)\mathbf1_n^T=nJ$, so $H_n^2=(I_n-J/n)^2=I_n-2J/n+J^2/n^2=I_n-J/n=H_n$. The formula for $H_nv$ in [F1] shows that its image is zero-sum; if $\mathbf1_n^Tv=0$, then $H_nv=v$. For any $v$, the residual $v-H_nv=(n^{-1}\mathbf1_n^Tv)\mathbf1_n$ is orthogonal to every zero-sum vector by [F2]. Hence $H_nv$ is the orthogonal projection of $v$ onto the zero-sum subspace.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, let
$T:V\to V$ be linear, and let $\mathcal E$ be an orthonormal basis of $V$. Write

$$A=[T]_{\mathcal E}^{\mathcal E}.$$

Then:

1. $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$.
2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is just $A^{\mathsf T}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], the matrix $A$ represents a self-adjoint map on $\mathbb R^p$ with its standard inner product; [F3] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_p$ ordered with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p$.

For any feasible $Q$, put $P=QQ^T$. Since $Q^TQ=I_q$, $P^T=P$ and $P^2=P$, so $u_j=Pu_j+(I-P)u_j$ is an orthogonal decomposition and $a_j:=u_j^TPu_j=\|Q^Tu_j\|_2^2=\|Pu_j\|_2^2$ lies in $[0,1]$. This decomposition gives $a_j=0$ exactly when $Pu_j=0$, and $a_j=1$ exactly when $Pu_j=u_j$. Also $\sum_{j=1}^p a_j=\operatorname{tr}(P)=q$ by [F4]. The frame trace equals $\operatorname{tr}(PA)$ by [F5]. If $U$ has columns $u_j$ and $\Lambda=U^TAU=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)$, [F5] and $UU^T=I$ give $\operatorname{tr}(PA)=\operatorname{tr}(U^TPAU)=\operatorname{tr}((U^TPU)\Lambda)=\sum_{j=1}^p\lambda_j a_j$.

Because $\lambda_j\ge\lambda_q$ for $j\le q$ and $\lambda_j\le\lambda_q$ for $j>q$, $\sum_{j=1}^p\lambda_j a_j\le\sum_{j=1}^q(\lambda_j a_j+\lambda_q(1-a_j))\le\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_j$. The first inequality uses $\sum_j a_j=q$; the second uses $0\le a_j\le1$ and $\lambda_j\ge\lambda_q$ for $j\le q$.

The first inequality in step 3.1 has nonnegative difference $\sum_{j>q}(\lambda_q-\lambda_j)a_j$, so equality requires $a_j=0$ whenever $\lambda_j<\lambda_q$. The second has nonnegative difference $\sum_{j\le q}(\lambda_j-\lambda_q)(1-a_j)$, so equality requires $a_j=1$ whenever $\lambda_j>\lambda_q$. By step 2.1, these conditions say the chosen subspace contains all higher-eigenvalue eigenspaces, is orthogonal to all lower-eigenvalue eigenspaces, and takes its remaining dimension in the $\lambda_q$ eigenspace. Conversely, each such subspace makes both differences zero. If $A=0$, all eigenvalues are zero and both differences vanish for every feasible $Q$, as does the stated equality condition.

Taking the first $q$ vectors of the eigenbasis from step 1.1 as the columns of $Q$ gives a feasible frame and makes the trace equal $\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_j$. Thus the upper bound is the attained maximum, with the stated equality cases.

For a finite data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n,p\ge1$, set $H_n=I_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$ and $X_c=H_nX$. For an integer $q$ with $1\le q\le p$, a rank-$q$ PCA frame is a matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ with $Q^TQ=I_q$. Its reconstruction is $X_cQQ^T$, and its squared Frobenius reconstruction error is

$$\|X_c-X_cQQ^T\|_F^2=\sum_{i<n}\sum_{j<p}(X_c-X_cQQ^T)_{ij}^2.$$

A rank-$q$ PCA solution is any frame minimizing this error over all such $Q$; its score matrix is $X_cQ$. A minimizing frame need not be unique when the relevant eigenvalues are tied.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p$, counted with multiplicity. For $1\le q\le p$ and every $Q\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ satisfying $Q^TQ=I_q$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)\le\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_j.$$

Equality is attained by taking the columns of $Q$ to be orthonormal eigenvectors for the $q$ largest eigenvalues. Equality holds exactly when the column space of $Q$ contains every eigenspace with eigenvalue greater than $\lambda_q$, is orthogonal to every eigenspace with eigenvalue less than $\lambda_q$, and uses a subspace of dimension $q-\#\{j:\lambda_j>\lambda_q\}$ from the eigenspace with eigenvalue $\lambda_q$.

derivations.claim: Put $C=X_c$ and $P=QQ^T$. Since $Q^TQ=I_q$, $P^T=P$ and $P^2=P$, so $C-CQQ^T=C(I-P)$ and $(I-P)^2=I-P$. By [F2] and [F5], $\|C(I-P)\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}((I-P)C^TC(I-P))$. Applying [F6] to cycle the first factor gives $\operatorname{tr}(C^TC(I-P)^2)=\operatorname{tr}(C^TC(I-P))$; then linearity gives $\operatorname{tr}(C^TC)-\operatorname{tr}(C^TCP)$. Applying [F6] again gives $\operatorname{tr}(C^TCP)=\operatorname{tr}(Q^TC^TCQ)$. Thus minimizing the reconstruction error is equivalent to maximizing $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TC^TCQ)$.

By [F3], choose right singular vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_p$ and corresponding left vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ such that $Cv_j=\sigma_j u_j$ for $j\le r$ and $Cv_j=0$ for $j>r$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}C$. For $i,j\le r$, [F4] gives $v_i^TC^TCv_j=(Cv_i)^T(Cv_j)=\sigma_i\sigma_j u_i^Tu_j$, which is $\sigma_j^2$ when $i=j$ and zero otherwise; for $j>r$ it is zero. Thus $C^TC$ has eigenvalues $\sigma_1^2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p^2\ge0$ in the basis $v_j$. Applying [F8] to $A=C^TC$ shows that the maximum trace is $\sum_{j=1}^q\sigma_j^2$, attained exactly by the top-eigenspace subspaces described in the statement. Therefore the minimum error is $\|C\|_F^2-\sum_{j=1}^q\sigma_j^2$.

Substituting [F7] into the last expression gives $\sum_{j=q+1}^p\sigma_j^2$. The SVD basis in [F3] supplies a feasible frame from the top $q$ right singular vectors, so the bound is attained. If $q=p$, the sum is empty and equals zero; if $\operatorname{rank}C\le q$, every term in the tail is zero.

For a requested dimension $q\ge1$, classical multidimensional scaling diagonalizes the real symmetric matrix $B$, retains up to the $q$ largest strictly positive eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$, and returns coordinates whose columns are $u_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}$. If fewer than $q$ positive eigenvalues exist, it returns only those positive-eigenvalue coordinates. For non-Euclidean dissimilarities this is a spectral procedure; it does not assert exact recovery of all entries of $D$.

self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

Let $n\ge0$, $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R^m$ be finite lists with $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=\langle y_i,y_j\rangle$ for every $1\le i,j\le n$, using the standard Euclidean inner products. The assignment $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i$ is a well-defined linear isometry from $\operatorname{span}\{x_i\}$ onto $\operatorname{span}\{y_i\}$; when $n=0$ both spans are zero spaces and the assignment is the unique zero map.

derivations.claim: For any permitted $D$, $D^{\circ2}$ is symmetric and $H_n$ is symmetric by [F2], so $B^T=B$. The standard coordinate basis is orthonormal for [F3], so [F4] makes $B$ self-adjoint and [F5] gives a real orthonormal eigendecomposition; this justifies the spectral step even when some eigenvalues are negative.

Suppose $D_{ij}=\|z_i-z_j\|_2$ and let $Z$ be the matrix with rows $z_i^T$. Put $s_i=\|z_i\|_2^2$. Expanding each squared distance with the coordinate inner product [F3] gives $D^{\circ2}=s\mathbf1_n^T+\mathbf1_ns^T-2ZZ^T$, hence $B=-\frac12H_n(s\mathbf1_n^T+\mathbf1_ns^T-2ZZ^T)H_n=H_nZZ^TH_n=Z_cZ_c^T$ because $H_n\mathbf1_n=0$ and $H_n^T=H_n$ by [F2]. For every $a$, $a^TBa=\sum_r((Z_c^Ta)_r)^2\ge0$ by the coordinate formula [F3], so $B$ is positive semidefinite; also $B\mathbf1_n=Z_cZ_c^T\mathbf1_n=0$. When $n=1$, $H_1=0$, so $Z_c=0$ and $B=0$.

In the Euclidean-distance case of step 1.2, $B$ is positive semidefinite. By [F5], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis; all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the zero-eigenvalue terms vanish and $B=U_+\Lambda_+U_+^T$, where $U_+$ contains exactly the positive-eigenvalue eigenvectors and $\Lambda_+$ is diagonal with strictly positive entries. If there are no positive eigenvalues, this is the empty decomposition and $B=0$. The classical-MDS coordinates from all positive eigenvalues are $Y=U_+\Lambda_+^{1/2}$, so $YY^T=B$. By step 1.2, $B\mathbf1_n=0$, and each column $u$ of $U_+$ with eigenvalue $\lambda>0$ satisfies $\lambda u^T\mathbf1_n=u^TB\mathbf1_n=0$; hence the rows of $Y$ are centered.

By [F2], row $i$ of $Z_c$ is $z_i-\bar z$, where $\bar z=n^{-1}\sum_i z_i$. For each $i,j$, the coordinate Gram identity gives $\|y_i-y_j\|_2^2=B_{ii}+B_{jj}-2B_{ij}=\|z_i-\bar z-(z_j-\bar z)\|_2^2=\|z_i-z_j\|_2^2=D_{ij}^2$. Both distances are nonnegative, so $\|y_i-y_j\|_2=D_{ij}$. The procedure retaining up to the requested dimension $q$ has the same Gram matrix when $q$ is at least the number of positive eigenvalues, so these equalities then hold for its returned coordinates.

The row configurations of $Z_c$ and $Y$ have the same Gram matrix $B$ by step 1.2 and step 2.1. Applying [F6] gives an isometry between their spans. The original rows of $Z$ differ from those of $Z_c$ by the common translation $\bar z$, so the original and embedded configurations are congruent after this translation. For a non-Euclidean $D$, step 1.1 still gives a symmetric spectral problem, but step 1.2 is unavailable and no exact-distance conclusion follows.

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, $n\ge2$, and $1\le k<n$. For each $i$, let $N_i$ be the first $k$ indices $j\ne i$ under the increasing lexicographic order of $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$, so equal distances are broken by sample index; the norm on $\mathbb R^p$ is $\|z\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p z_a^2)^{1/2}$. The local affine reconstruction weights are the vector $w_i=(w_{ij})_{j\in N_i}\in\mathbb R^k$ minimizing

$$\left\|x_i-\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}x_j\right\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}=1,$$

Among all minimizers, choose the one of smallest Euclidean norm $\|w_i\|_2=(\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. This minimum-norm rule fixes the weights even when the local covariance matrix is singular.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

derivations.claim: Let $w^0=(1,0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb R^k$, let $L=\{z\in\mathbb R^k:\sum_s z_s=0\}$, and define $T:L\to\mathbb R^p$ by $Tz=\sum_s z_sx_{j_s}$. Every feasible $w$ has a unique form $w=w^0+z$ with $z\in L$, and its residual is $x_i-x_{j_1}-Tz$. Thus the constrained problem is an ordinary finite-dimensional least-squares problem for $T$ on the inner-product subspace $L$.

By [F2], choose a least-squares minimizer $z_0\in L$ and all minimizers are $z_0+N$, where $N=\ker T\subseteq L$. Therefore all feasible minimizing weights form the nonempty affine set $w^0+z_0+N$. In the degenerate case $T=0$, $z_0=0$ is a minimizer and $N=L$, so this set contains every feasible weight.

Put $w_*=w^0+z_0$. By [F4], decompose $w_*=u+v$ with $u\in N$ and $v\in N^\perp$ in $\mathbb R^k$. Since $-u\in N$, $v=w_*-u$ remains in the affine minimizer set. For any other minimizer $v+h$ with $h\in N$, orthogonality gives $\|v+h\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|h\|_2^2$, which is at least $\|v\|_2^2$ with equality only if $h=0$. Hence $v$ is the unique minimum-norm minimizer. When $k=1$, $L=N=\{0\}$ and this gives the unique feasible weight $w^0=(1)$.

The proof applies the least-squares existence result once to this fixed finite-dimensional problem and uses a finite orthogonal decomposition; it selects no sequence of approximate minimizers and uses no Countable Choice.

Input: a data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n\ge2$, a neighbor count $1\le k<n$, and an output dimension $1\le q<n$, using $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p v_a^2)^{1/2}$. For every row point $x_i$, select the first $k$ other sample indices ordered by $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$ and use the minimum-Euclidean-norm affine least-squares weights on that neighborhood, with weights summing to $1$. Form $W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ by placing those weights in the selected columns of row $i$ and zeros elsewhere; every row of $W$ then sums to $1$. If $\ker(I_n-W)\ne\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_n\}$, return the status “constant kernel not isolated” and do not specify an embedding. Otherwise put $M=(I_n-W)^T(I_n-W)$ and return any $Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$ minimizing

$$\operatorname{tr}(Y^TMY)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Y^T\mathbf1_n=0,\qquad Y^TY=I_q,$$

where $\operatorname{tr}$ is the sum of diagonal entries. Equivalently, take orthonormal eigenvectors for the $q$ smallest positive eigenvalues of $M$. Ties allow multiple outputs. This finite-matrix procedure makes no guarantee of manifold recovery or consistency.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p$, counted with multiplicity. For $1\le q\le p$ and every $Q\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ satisfying $Q^TQ=I_q$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)\le\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_j.$$

Equality is attained by taking the columns of $Q$ to be orthonormal eigenvectors for the $q$ largest eigenvalues. Equality holds exactly when the column space of $Q$ contains every eigenspace with eigenvalue greater than $\lambda_q$, is orthogonal to every eigenspace with eigenvalue less than $\lambda_q$, and uses a subspace of dimension $q-\#\{j:\lambda_j>\lambda_q\}$ from the eigenspace with eigenvalue $\lambda_q$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: Put $A=I_n-W$. Then $A\mathbf1_n=0$ by [F1], and $M=A^TA$ is symmetric with $M\mathbf1_n=0$. For every $v$, $v^TMv=(Av)^T(Av)=\sum_r(Av)_r^2\ge0$ by [F2]. Also $Mv=0$ implies $0=v^TMv=\sum_r(Av)_r^2$, hence $Av=0$; conversely $Av=0$ implies $Mv=0$. Therefore $\ker M=\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_n\}$.

By [F4], $\mathbb R^n=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_n\}\oplus S$ for $S=\mathbf1_n^\perp$, and [F3] gives an orthonormal basis matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-1)}$ for $S$. Symmetry and $M\mathbf1_n=0$ imply $M(S)\subseteq S$, because $\mathbf1_n^TMv=(M\mathbf1_n)^Tv=0$ for $v\in S$. The restriction has matrix $R=E^TME$, which is symmetric and positive definite: if $c\ne0$, then $Ec\in S\setminus\{0\}$, so $Ec\notin\ker M$ by step 1.1 and $c^TRc=(Ec)^TM(Ec)=\sum_r(AEc)_r^2>0$. Its eigenvalues are therefore $0<\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_{n-1}$.

For every feasible $Y$, its columns lie in $S$, so $Y=EQ$ with $Q=E^TY$ and $Q^TQ=I_q$. Substitution gives $Y^TMY=Q^TRQ$, hence $\operatorname{tr}(Y^TMY)=\operatorname{tr}(Q^TRQ)$ by [F6]. Apply [F5] to $-R$, whose eigenvalues in descending order are $-\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge-\mu_{n-1}$. It follows that $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TRQ)\ge\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j$, with equality exactly for the q-dimensional bottom eigenspaces, including arbitrary choices inside a tie.

Taking $Q$ to have orthonormal columns spanning q bottom eigendirections of $R$ and setting $Y=EQ$ satisfies both constraints and attains the bound in step 3.1. This proves the minimum and its equality cases.

For a finite data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n,p\ge1$, set $H_n=I_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$ and $X_c=H_nX$. For an integer $q$ with $1\le q\le p$, a rank-$q$ PCA frame is a matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ with $Q^TQ=I_q$. Its reconstruction is $X_cQQ^T$, and its squared Frobenius reconstruction error is

$$\|X_c-X_cQQ^T\|_F^2=\sum_{i<n}\sum_{j<p}(X_c-X_cQQ^T)_{ij}^2.$$

A rank-$q$ PCA solution is any frame minimizing this error over all such $Q$; its score matrix is $X_cQ$. A minimizing frame need not be unique when the relevant eigenvalues are tied.

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $n,p\ge1$, let $X_c=(I_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T)X$, and let $1\le q\le p$. Write $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p\ge0$ for the singular values of $X_c$, padding by zeros after its rank. Among all $Q\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ with $Q^TQ=I_q$, the minimum of $\|X_c-X_cQQ^T\|_F^2$ is

$$\sum_{j=q+1}^{p}\sigma_j^2.$$

A frame is minimizing exactly when its column space contains every eigenspace of $X_c^TX_c$ with eigenvalue greater than $\sigma_q^2$, is orthogonal to every eigenspace with eigenvalue less than $\sigma_q^2$, and uses the remaining dimension inside the eigenspace with eigenvalue $\sigma_q^2$. In particular a choice of $q$ right singular vectors for the $q$ largest singular values is minimizing; ties can give different minimizing subspaces.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with nonnegative entries and zero diagonal, and write $D^{\circ2}$ for the matrix with entries $(D^{\circ2})_{ij}=D_{ij}^2$. Define $H_n=I_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$ and the centered matrix

$$B:=-\frac12H_nD^{\circ2}H_n.$$

For a requested dimension $q\ge1$, classical multidimensional scaling diagonalizes the real symmetric matrix $B$, retains up to the $q$ largest strictly positive eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$, and returns coordinates whose columns are $u_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}$. If fewer than $q$ positive eigenvalues exist, it returns only those positive-eigenvalue coordinates. For non-Euclidean dissimilarities this is a spectral procedure; it does not assert exact recovery of all entries of $D$.

Let $n\ge1$. For every symmetric nonnegative zero-diagonal dissimilarity matrix $D$, the matrix $B=-\frac12H_nD^{\circ2}H_n$ used by classical multidimensional scaling is symmetric and has a real orthonormal eigendecomposition, though it may have negative eigenvalues. If $D_{ij}=\|z_i-z_j\|_2$ for points $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^d$, where $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^d v_a^2)^{1/2}$, then $B=Z_cZ_c^T$ for the centered row-data matrix $Z_c=H_nZ$, so $B$ is positive semidefinite. The coordinates formed from all positive eigenvalues reproduce every pairwise distance exactly; if the requested embedding dimension is at least the number of positive eigenvalues, the truncated procedure is exact. The centered configurations obtained from $Z$ and these coordinates are related by a linear isometry between their spans, so the original configurations agree up to translation and Euclidean isometry of their affine spans.

derivations.claim: Put $u=(1,1,-2)^T$ and $v=(1,-1,0)^T$. Both are zero-sum, so $H_3u=u$ and $H_3v=v$. Thus $w=u+8v$ satisfies $w^TBw=19+16(-8)+64=-45<0$.

By [F2], $B$ is symmetric and has an orthonormal eigenbasis. If every eigenvalue were nonnegative, expressing $w$ in that eigenbasis would give $w^TBw\ge0$, contradicting step 1.1. Therefore $B$ has a negative eigenvalue.

The stated triangle inequality fails, since $D_{13}+D_{12}=2<D_{23}=3$, so no Euclidean point configuration realizes $D$. This matches the negative eigenvalue and the Euclidean-only exactness hypothesis of [F2].

For each $i$, let $N_i$ be the first $k$ indices $j\ne i$ under the increasing lexicographic order of $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$, so equal distances are broken by sample index; the norm on $\mathbb R^p$ is $\|z\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p z_a^2)^{1/2}$. The local affine reconstruction weights are the vector $w_i=(w_{ij})_{j\in N_i}\in\mathbb R^k$ minimizing

$$\left\|x_i-\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}x_j\right\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}=1,$$

Among all minimizers, choose the one of smallest Euclidean norm $\|w_i\|_2=(\sum_{j\in N_i}w_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. This minimum-norm rule fixes the weights even when the local covariance matrix is singular.

Fix $x_i\in\mathbb R^p$ and a nonempty finite neighbor list $N_i=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ of distinct indices. The constrained problem

$$\min_{w\in\mathbb R^k}\left\|x_i-\sum_{s=1}^k w_sx_{j_s}\right\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{s=1}^k w_s=1$$

has a nonempty affine set of minimizers, and exactly one member of that set has smallest Euclidean norm. Thus the minimum-norm rule in finite LLE defines one weight vector even when the local covariance matrix is singular. This conclusion uses no choice axiom.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with nonnegative entries and zero diagonal, and write $D^{\circ2}$ for the matrix with entries $(D^{\circ2})_{ij}=D_{ij}^2$. Define $H_n=I_n-n^{-1}\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^T$ and the centered matrix

$$B:=-\frac12H_nD^{\circ2}H_n.$$

For a requested dimension $q\ge1$, classical multidimensional scaling diagonalizes the real symmetric matrix $B$, retains up to the $q$ largest strictly positive eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$, and returns coordinates whose columns are $u_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}$. If fewer than $q$ positive eigenvalues exist, it returns only those positive-eigenvalue coordinates. For non-Euclidean dissimilarities this is a spectral procedure; it does not assert exact recovery of all entries of $D$.

Let $n\ge1$. For every symmetric nonnegative zero-diagonal dissimilarity matrix $D$, the matrix $B=-\frac12H_nD^{\circ2}H_n$ used by classical multidimensional scaling is symmetric and has a real orthonormal eigendecomposition, though it may have negative eigenvalues. If $D_{ij}=\|z_i-z_j\|_2$ for points $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^d$, where $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^d v_a^2)^{1/2}$, then $B=Z_cZ_c^T$ for the centered row-data matrix $Z_c=H_nZ$, so $B$ is positive semidefinite. The coordinates formed from all positive eigenvalues reproduce every pairwise distance exactly; if the requested embedding dimension is at least the number of positive eigenvalues, the truncated procedure is exact. The centered configurations obtained from $Z$ and these coordinates are related by a linear isometry between their spans, so the original configurations agree up to translation and Euclidean isometry of their affine spans.

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ with $n\ge2$, using the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p v_a^2)^{1/2}$. For $1\le k<n$, the deterministic $k$-nearest-neighbor list $N_k(i)$ consists of the first $k$ indices $j\ne i$ when the other indices are ordered by increasing pair $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$ lexicographically; thus equal distances are broken by increasing sample index. All graphs below have vertex set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The **union symmetrization** has edge $\{i,j\}$ when $j\in N_k(i)$ or $i\in N_k(j)$; the **mutual symmetrization** has edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when both inclusions hold. Each included edge may be assigned weight $\|x_i-x_j\|_2$. For a radius $r>0$, the radius graph has edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\|x_i-x_j\|_2\le r$ for $1\le i<j\le n$. An undirected graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a finite edge path.

Input: a finite data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n\ge2$, an embedding dimension $q\ge1$, and either a $k$-nearest-neighbor parameter $1\le k<n$ with an explicit union or mutual symmetrization choice, or a radius $r>0$. Use $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p v_a^2)^{1/2}$; for the $k$-nearest-neighbor option, each neighbor list orders candidates by increasing $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$, so equal distances are broken by sample index. Construct the selected undirected graph and give each edge $\{i,j\}$ weight $\|x_i-x_j\|_2$. If the graph is disconnected, return the status “disconnected” and do not claim finite all-pairs graph distances. If it is connected, define $d_G(i,j)$ as the minimum total edge weight over all paths from $i$ to $j$; because the graph is finite with nonnegative edge weights, a minimum occurs among its finitely many simple paths. Form the symmetric dissimilarity matrix $D_G=(d_G(i,j))$ and apply classical multidimensional scaling to $D_G$ with requested dimension $q$. This finite procedure makes no guarantee that graph distances accurately approximate manifold geodesics or that the output recovers a manifold.

Input: a data matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n\ge2$, a neighbor count $1\le k<n$, and an output dimension $1\le q<n$, using $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^p v_a^2)^{1/2}$. For every row point $x_i$, select the first $k$ other sample indices ordered by $(\|x_i-x_j\|_2,j)$ and use the minimum-Euclidean-norm affine least-squares weights on that neighborhood, with weights summing to $1$. Form $W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ by placing those weights in the selected columns of row $i$ and zeros elsewhere; every row of $W$ then sums to $1$. If $\ker(I_n-W)\ne\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_n\}$, return the status “constant kernel not isolated” and do not specify an embedding. Otherwise put $M=(I_n-W)^T(I_n-W)$ and return any $Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$ minimizing

$$\operatorname{tr}(Y^TMY)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Y^T\mathbf1_n=0,\qquad Y^TY=I_q,$$

where $\operatorname{tr}$ is the sum of diagonal entries. Equivalently, take orthonormal eigenvectors for the $q$ smallest positive eigenvalues of $M$. Ties allow multiple outputs. This finite-matrix procedure makes no guarantee of manifold recovery or consistency.

Let $W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $W\mathbf1_n=\mathbf1_n$, put $M=(I_n-W)^T(I_n-W)$, and assume $\ker(I_n-W)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_n\}$. Let $0<\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_{n-1}$ be the eigenvalues of $M$ restricted to the zero-sum subspace $\mathbf1_n^\perp$. For $1\le q<n$, the minimum of $\operatorname{tr}(Y^TMY)$ over $Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$ with $Y^T\mathbf1_n=0$ and $Y^TY=I_q$ is $\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j$. The minimum is attained by taking the columns of $Y$ to be orthonormal eigenvectors for the $q$ smallest positive eigenvalues; when eigenvalues tie, the minimizing subspace may vary inside the tied eigenspace. The trace is the sum of diagonal entries.

The unit vector $u_x=(-1,1,1,-1)^T/2$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$, as is $u_y=(-1,-1,1,1)^T/2$; the other two eigenvalues are zero. Thus the x-coordinate choice $Y_M=u_x$ is a valid q=1 classical-MDS output, and it has repeated pairs $y_1=y_4$ and $y_2=y_3$.

With one neighbor per row, each LLE weight is $1$. Thus $W_{12}=W_{21}=W_{32}=W_{41}=1$ and other entries are zero; the equations $Wy=y$ force $y_1=y_2=y_3=y_4$, so the kernel is exactly the constant vectors. The matrix is $M=(I-W)^T(I-W)=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2&0&-1\\-2&3&-1&0\\0&-1&1&0\\-1&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Its symmetric subspace vectors $(c,c,d,d)$ have eigenvalues $0,2$. On antisymmetric vectors $(c,-c,-d,d)$ it acts by $(c,d)\mapsto(5c-d,d-c)$, whose characteristic equation is $\lambda^2-6\lambda+4=0$, giving eigenvalues $3-\sqrt5$ and $3+\sqrt5$. Hence the lowest positive eigenvalue is $3-\sqrt5$ with eigenvector $(a,-a,-1,1)^T$, where $a=\sqrt5-2\in(0,1)$.

The distances from each square vertex to its two side-neighbors tie at $1$. By [F3], the neighbor lists are $N_1=(2)$, $N_2=(1)$, $N_3=(2)$, and $N_4=(1)$; the union graph has the stated edges and is the path $4-1-2-3$. Its graph distances are exactly the line distances of the centered vector $Y_I=(-1/2,1/2,3/2,-3/2)^T$. Since this graph-distance matrix is Euclidean in one dimension, [F2] shows that ISOMAP’s q=1 classical-MDS output is congruent to $Y_I$. In particular its distance between vertices 1 and 4 is $1$, unlike the zero MDS distance in step 1.1.

The LLE coordinate has four distinct values, unlike $Y_M$, so it is not congruent to the classical-MDS output. Its sorted consecutive gaps are proportional to $1-a,2a,1-a$, and these are not all equal: $2a=1-a$ would imply $3\sqrt5=7$, contradicting $45\ne49$ after squaring. The ISOMAP line has equal consecutive gaps, so LLE is not congruent to ISOMAP either. The distinct distance $d_{14}=1$ in ISOMAP and $d_{14}=0$ in classical MDS already separates those two outputs.

For a symmetric nonnegative zero-diagonal dissimilarity matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge2$, and a target dimension $q\ge1$, use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{a=1}^q v_a^2)^{1/2}$. The **metric stress** of centered coordinates $Y=(y_1^T,\ldots,y_n^T)^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$, with $\mathbf1_n^TY=0$, is

$$S_D(Y):=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\bigl(D_{ij}-\|y_i-y_j\|_2\bigr)^2.$$

Metric stress MDS is the separate optimization problem of minimizing $S_D(Y)$ over such centered $Y$. It is a distance-based, generally nonconvex objective and does not define the positive-eigenvalue solution used by classical multidimensional scaling; no solver convergence or global-optimizer guarantee is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: For $Y(t)=(t,-t)$, the sole distance is $|t-(-t)|=2|t|$, so [F1] gives $f(t)=(1-2|t|)^2$.

A convex function must satisfy the midpoint inequality $f(0)\le\tfrac12f(-a)+\tfrac12f(a)$. At $a=1/4$, $f(0)=1$ and $f(-a)=f(a)=(1-1/2)^2=1/4$, so the midpoint inequality fails. Hence this valid stress objective is nonconvex.
